p: The cat of Norse legend. A mountain-climbing giant in a weatherproof coat.
s: The Norwegian Forest Cat, called the Wegie for short, is the stuff of Viking legend. These big longhairs have lived in Norway for centuries, and they appear in Norse myth as the cats that pulled the goddess Freya's chariot. King Olav V named the breed the official cat of Norway.

It is built for a cold, wet climate. A long double coat with a dense woolly underlayer sheds rain and snow, topped by a full ruff, tufted lynx-tipped ears, and a long bushy tail. Big and muscular, the Wegie is a powerful climber that descends trees head-first.

For all its wild looks, the temperament is gentle and friendly. The Norwegian Forest Cat is calm, patient, and sociable, fond of its family without being demanding, and happy to watch the household from a high perch.

It is often confused with the Maine Coon, and the two share a similar size and rugged build, but they developed an ocean apart and differ in head shape and coat. The Wegie is slow to mature, reaching full size at around five years.

The Wegie is a calm, friendly giant that likes to survey its home from up high. It is sociable without being clingy, patient with children and other pets, and content to spend part of the day on its own, though it enjoys company when it is offered.

The water-shedding double coat needs regular brushing, with a heavy molt in spring that calls for daily attention. The breed is sturdy but can carry the heart condition HCM, a kidney condition, and a rare metabolic disorder called GSD IV, so reputable breeders test for them.
rc: Norway's legendary forest cat, in CFA's top fifteen
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the forests of Norway, where it lived for centuries, and tied to Norse myth as Freya's cat.
A Natural Breed
An ancient Scandinavian forest cat shaped by climate, later named the national cat of Norway.
Good to Know
Sociable and easygoing, it loves to climb and perch. The thick coat needs regular brushing, especially in spring.
Coat & Color
A long, water-shedding double coat with a ruff, tufted ears, and bushy tail, in many colors and patterns.
By the Numbers
Reaches full size at around five years. Similar to the Maine Coon but a distinct, separately developed breed.
Living with One
Offer tall perches, regular brushing, and easygoing company. The Wegie is independent but affectionate on its own terms.
Health Notes
Can carry the heart condition HCM and a rare metabolic disorder, so choose breeders who screen their lines.
d: The Norwegian Forest Cat wears a waterproof coat over a wool undercoat.
Norse myth gave the goddess Freya a chariot pulled by two giant cats.
It takes up to five years to reach full size and full glory.
Nothing says winter like a Wegie asleep in the hay, tail over its nose.
The best seat in the barn is the doorway, with a view and no wind.
King Olav V is said to have made it Norway's official cat. Ask your friends.
After the snow and the chores, a Wegie tucks in one paw and sleeps.
lw: The path is white and the cabin light is on.

A Norwegian Forest Cat has crossed this snow a thousand times. It walks without hurry, tail high, as if the forest were its own front yard. When it reaches the door, it does not ask to come in. It waits, because it knows the warm room is already waiting for it.

p: France's smiling blue. A quiet, woolly cat with a monastery legend.
s: The Chartreux is France's own blue cat, old enough to come wrapped in legend. Stories tie it to the Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse, and it has been part of French life for centuries, praised by writers and treated as a national treasure.

The coat is its trademark. A dense, woolly, water-resistant blue-grey coat stands slightly away from the body, and a rounded head with full cheeks and a gently upturned mouth gives the breed its famous smile. Bright copper or orange eyes complete the look.

It is a robust, powerful cat on surprisingly fine legs, sometimes described as a potato on toothpicks. The Chartreux is an excellent mouser, calm and observant, and notably quiet, with some individuals barely making a sound.
The temperament is gentle and undemanding. Chartreux are devoted but reserved, attaching to their families while keeping a dignified, easygoing calm, content to follow quietly from room to room.

The Chartreux is a quiet, gentle companion that bonds closely while keeping a dignified calm. It is an excellent, patient mouser, content to follow its people from room to room and settle nearby, and it is notably silent, with some cats barely making a sound.

The dense, woolly coat is best cared for by combing and hand-grooming rather than heavy brushing, which can spoil its texture, and it sheds seasonally. The breed is robust and long-lived, though some lines can carry hip problems and a urinary tendency, so reputable breeders screen and owners keep it lean.
rc: France's ancient blue cat, with a woolly coat and a quiet smile
f: Origin of the Name
Linked by legend to the Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse in France.
An Ancient Breed
A centuries-old French cat, celebrated in literature and regarded as a national treasure.
Good to Know
Calm, quiet, and devoted, it bonds closely while staying undemanding. A fine, observant mouser that rarely makes noise.
Coat & Color
A dense, woolly, water-resistant blue-grey coat with copper or orange eyes and a smiling expression.
By the Numbers
Robust and powerful on fine legs, and one of the quietest of all breeds.
Living with One
Comb the woolly coat by hand and offer calm company. The Chartreux is quiet, devoted, and easy to live with.
Health Notes
Hardy and long-lived, though some lines carry hip issues, so choose screened breeders and keep the cat lean and active.
d: The Chartreux is a French cat with a woolly blue coat and copper eyes.
Legend ties them to Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse.
Many Chartreux seldom meow. A few never make a sound at all.
Any pot big enough will do. A Chartreux checks the fit and moves in.
Sit where the sun lands. Wait. The day will come to you.
They are called the smiling blue cats of France. Look at the mouth.
Even the busiest garden helper naps against the pots when work is done.
lw: The greenhouse glows and the frost is winning outside.

The Chartreux has made its rounds. It has checked every pot, every shelf, and every sunny square of floor. Now it settles on the burlap and lets the string lights count the hours. Tomorrow there will be more to inspect. Tonight, the smile stays.

p: Turkey's silken dancer. An elegant longhair with a national pedigree.
s: The Turkish Angora is one of the oldest known longhaired breeds, named for Ankara, the Turkish city once called Angora. It has charmed Europe since at least the 1600s, and Turkey treasures it enough to run a preservation program at the Ankara Zoo.

It is built for grace. A fine-boned, athletic body carries a silky single coat that flows when the cat moves, with a plumed tail and a delicate wedge-shaped face. The classic Angora is a brilliant white, often with eyes of blue, amber, or one of each.

The personality is lively and bold. Angoras are playful, clever, and athletic, fond of high perches and of being the center of attention, and they bond closely and follow their people from room to room.

One trait needs care. White, blue-eyed Angoras can carry a gene linked to deafness, especially on the blue-eyed side, so odd-eyed cats may hear on only one side. The single coat is silky and far easier to groom than a double one.

The Turkish Angora is a lively, bold cat that bonds closely and likes to be in charge of the room. It is playful and athletic, fond of high perches and water, and so attached to its people that it follows them about and tends to choose a favorite.

The silky single coat has no dense undercoat, so it rarely mats and needs only weekly brushing. The breed is generally healthy, but white, blue-eyed cats can carry a gene linked to deafness, and some lines carry the heart condition HCM and a rare neurological disorder, so reputable breeders test.
rc: Turkey's ancient national longhair, a treasure of the Ankara Zoo
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Ankara, the Turkish capital once called Angora, its home for centuries.
An Ancient Breed
One of the oldest longhairs, prized in Europe since the 1600s and preserved today in Turkey.
Good to Know
Active and attention-loving, it enjoys climbing and play. The single coat is easy to groom, with no dense undercoat to mat.
Coat & Color
A long, silky single coat with a plumed tail, classically pure white, also in many colors and patterns.
By the Numbers
White blue-eyed cats can carry a deafness gene, so odd-eyed Angoras may be deaf on the blue-eyed side.
Living with One
Give it heights, play, and attention. The Angora is bold and devoted and likes to run the household.
Health Notes
White blue-eyed cats can be deaf. Some lines carry the heart condition HCM, so choose breeders who screen their cats.
d: Angora is the old name for Ankara, the Turkish capital. This is the Ankara cat.
The Ankara Zoo runs a preservation program for the breed.
The silky coat has no dense undercoat, so it rarely mats.
A white cat in a white blanket is a magic trick. Look for the eyes.
Be elegant. Be curious. Stay near the sunniest window.
A white Angora may have one blue eye and one amber. Ask your friends.
The head goes down on the basket and the whole house gets quiet.
lw: The sunroom turns gold, and the snow outside turns rose.

The Turkish Angora has run, leapt, and inspected every lemon on the tree. Now the plume of a tail curls around it like a scarf. It has been loved in Ankara for centuries, and it knows exactly how to be admired. It only asks that the cushion stay warm.

p: A brick wrapped in silk. A glossy, golden-eyed cat that adores its people.
s: The modern Burmese traces to a single cat. In the 1930s a small brown cat named Wong Mau was brought from Burma to the United States, and a careful breeding program built an entire breed around her warm sable coat and sweet nature.

It is deceptively solid. The Burmese looks compact and rounded but feels surprisingly heavy in the hand, leading to the old description of a brick wrapped in silk. The short, glossy coat lies close to a muscular body, set off by large, round, golden-yellow eyes.

The temperament is its glory. Burmese are devoted, people-oriented, and endlessly affectionate, often called the most dog-like of cats for the way they follow, greet, and insist on laps. They stay playful and kittenish well into adulthood.
They do not like to be alone and thrive in busy, loving homes. The breed also helped create the Tonkinese through crosses with the Siamese, and it comes in sable and several diluted shades.

A Burmese is famously people-dependent. It wants laps, shoulders, and conversation, follows its owners from room to room, and stays playful and kitten-like for years, which makes it a delightful companion and a poor choice for anyone away from home all day.

The short, satiny coat needs only a weekly wipe, but the breed carries a few risks worth knowing, including dental disease, diabetes, and, in some lines, a serious skull deformity and a condition that causes painful sensitivity, so reputable breeders test carefully.
rc: The devoted sable cat descended from a single import named Wong Mau
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Burma, the homeland of Wong Mau, the foundation cat brought to the United States in the 1930s.
A Founding Cat
Nearly the entire breed descends from Wong Mau, bred to fix her warm brown coat and sweet temperament.
Good to Know
Affectionate and people-focused, it wants company and laps and dislikes being left alone for long.
Coat & Color
A short, satiny, close-lying coat, classically warm sable brown, also in dilute shades, with golden eyes.
By the Numbers
A parent of the Tonkinese through crosses with the Siamese, and a long-standing favorite for its dog-like devotion.
Living with One
Give it laps, play, and company. The Burmese is devoted and social and unhappy left alone for long stretches.
Health Notes
Easy to groom, but watch for dental disease and diabetes and choose breeders who screen for known inherited conditions.
d: Most Burmese cats trace back to one brown cat named Wong Mau.
Wong Mau came from Burma to the United States in the 1930s.
Burmese weigh more than they look. Fans call them bricks wrapped in silk.
Your journal is now a cat bed. Write around the cat.
A warm mug, a cold window, and one good view. That is enough.
A Burmese talks like a Siamese, only softer. Ask your friends.
A quilt, a fire, and a Burmese asleep on your side of the bed.
lw: The lamp is on, and the snow keeps falling.

The Burmese has followed you from room to room all week. It has sat on your book, your sweater, and your plans. Now it curls into the quilt with a sigh, content to be exactly where you are. A heavy little heart, warm all the way through.

p: Russia's rugged forest cat. A powerful triple-coated giant with a tender streak.
s: The Siberian is Russia's native cat and its national treasure, a hardy longhair that survived centuries of brutal winters in the forests and villages of Siberia. It is an ancient natural breed, not a designed one, and it shows in every line of its powerful body.

That body is built for cold. A dense, water-resistant triple coat, a full neck ruff, and a bushy tail let it shrug off snow, and big tufted paws carry it over it. Under the fur it is muscular and surprisingly heavy, an athletic jumper that lands like a cat half its size.
Siberians are slow to mature, taking up to five years to fill out. They are playful, fearless, and dog-like, often fetching toys, following their people, and taking a curious interest in water.

They carry a useful reputation as well. Many allergy sufferers report tolerating Siberians better than other cats, since the breed tends to produce less of the main cat allergen, though no cat is truly safe for every allergic person.

A Siberian fits an active household. It is playful, fearless, and athletic, a strong jumper that enjoys games, heights, and even water, and it stays sociable and dog-like with family and guests alike. It is slow to mature, filling out over about five years.

The thick triple coat is less work than it looks, needing a thorough brush a couple of times a week and more during the heavy seasonal shed. The breed is generally healthy, though like many large cats it can carry the heart condition HCM, so responsible breeders test their lines.
rc: Russia's national cat, in CFA's top fifteen
f: Origin of The Name
Named for Siberia, the vast cold region of Russia where the breed developed in the wild and in villages.
A Natural Breed
An ancient forest cat shaped by harsh winters, not by breeders, and named the national cat of Russia.
Good To Know
Active, agile, and people-focused, it enjoys play and even water. The thick coat needs regular brushing, more during seasonal shedding.
Coat & Color
A long, water-resistant triple coat with a ruff and bushy tail, in a wide range of colors and patterns.
By the Numbers
Slow to mature at up to five years, and often better tolerated by people with allergies, though never truly hypoallergenic.
Living With One
Give it play, climbing, and company. The Siberian is robust, friendly, and happy in a busy family home.
Health Notes
Brush a few times a week, more in shedding season. Can carry the heart condition HCM, so favor screened breeders.
d: The Siberian is Russia's native cat and wears a triple coat built for snow.
Forests and villages shaped it over centuries. No breeder designed that ruff.
It takes up to five years to fill out. That is a lot of cat still growing.
Belly up on the rug means the room is warm and nobody is a threat.
A thick coat is only a start. The best warmth is a rug beside the stove.
Siberians fetch toys and poke at faucets. Ask who stole the plaid blanket.
Snow at the window, a stove behind, and a big green-eyed cat watching it fall.
lw: The lanterns are lit and the last light goes pink over the pines.
The Siberian sits on the porch rail, ruff full of snow and tail wrapped like a scarf. It has watched the whole winter arrive and minds none of it. Soon it will go in to the stove.

p: The cat that looks like a tiny mountain lion. Ancient, athletic, and endlessly busy.
s: The Abyssinian looks like it stepped off the wall of an Egyptian tomb, and that resemblance helped build its legend. It is one of the oldest breeds in the fancy. Its true origins likely lie around the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia, but it took its name from Abyssinia, modern Ethiopia, where early show cats were said to come from.

The signature is the coat. Each hair is banded with several colors, a pattern called ticking, which gives the warm ruddy coat a glowing, wild-rabbit shimmer that shifts as the cat moves. The lithe body, large ears, and almond eyes complete the look of a miniature cougar.

Abyssinians are pure motion. They are athletic, curious, and busy, forever climbing to the highest shelf, opening cupboards, and supervising every task in the house. Owners call them the clowns of the cat world, and a bored Aby will invent its own entertainment.

For all that energy they are deeply people-oriented, less of a lap cat and more of a constant companion that wants to be in the room and in the action. CFA recognized the breed in 1906, and it has been a beloved fixture of the fancy ever since.

An Abyssinian needs a job, or it will appoint itself one. It is among the most active and clever of breeds, forever climbing, exploring, and helping with whatever you are doing, and it does best with tall perches, puzzle toys, and ideally a feline companion to match its energy.

The short coat is wash-and-wear, needing only an occasional brush, but the breed carries a few watch-points. Responsible breeders test for a blood disorder called PK deficiency, for an inherited eye condition, and for dental disease, all of which can run in the line. A fit, lean Aby tends to stay sprightly into old age.
f: Origin of The Name
Named for Abyssinia, the old name for Ethiopia, where the first show cats were reported, though its real roots lie farther east.
An Ancient Look
Its build and ticked coat echo the cats of ancient Egyptian art, which fed its romantic origin story.
Good To Know
High-energy and clever, the Aby needs climbing space, toys, and company. It is interactive rather than a lap cat and dislikes being idle.
Coat & Color
A short, close coat in which each hair is banded, giving a warm ticked shimmer, classically in ruddy and other warm tones.
By the Numbers
Recognized by CFA in 1906 and one of the oldest breeds in the registry.
Living With One
Give it height, puzzles, and company. The Aby is an athletic busybody that grows restless and loud when bored.
Health Notes
Easy to groom, but ask breeders about screening for the blood disorder PK deficiency and for eye and dental issues.
d: Abyssinian hairs are banded with several colors. That pattern is called ticking.
Named for Abyssinia, though the breed's roots may lie nearer the Indian Ocean.
An Aby can reach the top shelf before you finish saying its name.
Everything high is a perch and everything closed is a puzzle. The Aby is thorough.
A busy mind needs a tall place to think. Give it a shelf and some books.
Ask who supervised the dinner, the laundry, and the mail. The Aby was there.
Even a clown naps. A warm cushion on a low shelf is a small peace.
lw: Lamplight on the stairs, and the house is finally still.
The Abyssinian has climbed, leapt, and checked every cupboard this week. Now it pauses on the bottom step, ears up, listening to the snow against the glass. One more look around, then bed.

p: The pixie of the cat world. A big-eared imp in a suit of soft waves.
s: The Devon Rex looks like it wandered in from a fairy tale. It turned up in Devon, England, in 1960, when a curly-coated kitten named Kirlee was born to a stray. That single mutation gave the breed its rippled coat and its unmistakable elfin face.

Everything about the head is oversized and charming. Huge low-set ears, wide cheekbones, big mischievous eyes, and a short muzzle give it a pixie or even alien look. The body is slender and the coat is short, soft, and wavy, sometimes so fine it feels like suede.

The personality is the real draw. Devons are clowns, endlessly playful, clever, and busy, famous for riding around on shoulders and wedging into warm laps. People call them a monkey in a catsuit, and they bond hard to their chosen people.

Because the coat is so thin, Devons love warmth and will seek out the sunniest spot or the nearest neck. They are sociable and food-motivated and stay kittenish for life. The breed is distinct from the Cornish Rex, which carries a different curl gene.

Life with a Devon is rarely dull. It is relentlessly social and busy, prone to following you, perching on shoulders, and stealing the warm spot the second you leave it. It learns tricks, plays fetch, and grows lonely if left alone for long, so a companion or a lively household suits it.

The thin coat needs little brushing but changes the care list in other ways. Devons feel the cold and seek warmth, their large ears need regular cleaning, and the skin can grow oily and want an occasional gentle bath. The breed can carry a muscle condition called spasticity, so health-tested lines matter.
rc: The 'pixie cat,' a playful star in the top five (CFA)
f: Origin of The Name
Named for Devon, the English county where the founding curly kitten was born, and Rex for its rippled, wavy coat.
A Natural Mutation
The whole breed descends from a single curly-coated kitten named Kirlee, born to a stray in 1960.
Good To Know
Affectionate to the point of clingy, the Devon wants to be with you and seeks warmth. It is active and clever and bores without play.
Coat & Color
A short, fine, wavy coat that can feel like suede, in any color or pattern. Some areas may be only lightly furred.
By the Numbers
Carries a different curl gene than the Cornish Rex. A steady favorite, often the most popular shorthaired breed on CFA's list.
Living With One
Give it warmth, company, and constant play. The Devon hates being alone and invents mischief if it is under-stimulated.
Health Notes
Clean the big ears regularly and bathe occasionally for oily skin. The breed can carry a muscle disorder, so choose tested lines.
d: The Devon Rex began in Devon, England, with one curly kitten named Kirlee.
Kirlee was born to a stray in 1960. That wavy coat started a whole breed.
Huge low ears, a coat like suede, and a mind full of mischief.
A Devon in the toolbox looks proud. The tools are now mostly decoration.
A thin coat makes warmth a mission. Find the stove, or find a neck.
Ask who is helping with the birdhouse. The Devon says it is a team effort.
A plaid scrap, a warm bench, and a pixie asleep in the day's last shavings.
lw: The shop is quiet and the snow is falling hard outside.
The Devon Rex has supervised every cut and cleaned up none of the shavings. Now it curls on the bench near the stove, ears folded low, finally still. Tomorrow it will be a monkey in a catsuit again.

p: The Sacred Cat of Burma. A gentle blue-eyed beauty in white gloves.
s: The Birman comes wrapped in legend. Known as the Sacred Cat of Burma, it stars in a temple myth in which a golden goddess turned a faithful white temple cat to gold and sapphire, leaving its paws white where they rested on a dying priest.

The look matches the story. A Birman wears a silky pointed coat in seal, blue, and other shades, deep blue eyes, and four pure white feet, the front pair like gloves and the back like gauntlets. The coat is long but silky enough to resist matting.
Its nature is as soft as its coat. Birmans are gentle, quiet, and affectionate, more placid than the Siamese they resemble, content to follow you around and settle nearby without making demands.

The breed nearly vanished in Europe during the Second World War, surviving in a tiny handful of cats before being carefully rebuilt. It should not be confused with the Burmese, a different breed entirely.

The Birman is a calm, gentle companion that suits a quieter home. It is affectionate without being demanding, gets on with children and other pets, and tends to greet its people softly and settle nearby rather than clamor for attention.

The silky single coat resists matting and needs only a couple of brushings a week. The breed is generally healthy, though some lines can carry the heart condition HCM and a kidney condition, so responsible breeders test, and the cat does best as a companionable indoor pet.
rc: The 'Sacred Cat of Burma,' a gloved and blue-eyed colorpoint
f: Origin of The Name
From its temple legend as the Sacred Cat of Burma, though the modern breed was developed in France.
A Temple Legend
Folklore ties its blue eyes and white paws to a goddess and a devoted temple cat.
Good To Know
Calm and companionable, it likes to be near its people without demanding attention. The silky coat resists matting but still needs brushing.
Coat & Color
A long, silky, pointed coat with deep blue eyes and four white feet, the back ones reaching higher like gauntlets.
By the Numbers
Nearly lost in Europe during the Second World War and rebuilt from only a handful of cats. Distinct from the Burmese.
Living With One
Brush a couple of times a week and offer calm company. The Birman is sweet, mellow, and easy to live with.
Health Notes
Generally sound, but some lines carry the heart condition HCM and a kidney condition, so favor screened breeders.
d: A Birman has blue eyes, a pointed coat, and four white feet like gloves.
Legend says a goddess gave the Sacred Cat of Burma sapphire eyes and white paws.
In Europe the breed nearly vanished during the Second World War.
A Birman does not demand. It finds the best chair and waits to be noticed.
A quiet cat in a warm room is its own kind of library.
Birman or Burmese? Different breeds. Only one has white gloves and sapphire eyes.
Head on a stack of old books, white paws tucked, and the fire doing its work.
lw: The fire is low and the library glows amber.

The Birman has followed you from chair to chair all week without asking for a thing. Now it settles into the leather, blue eyes closing, white paws tucked under. A gentle companion, soft as the coat it wears.

p: The bald extrovert. A warm, wrinkled lapcat that acts more like a clingy toddler.
s: The Sphynx looks engineered in a lab, but it is an accident of nature. The breed traces to a hairless kitten born in Toronto in 1966, and breeders worked to build a healthy line around that single mutation. The result is a cat that is famous for what it does not have.

It is not truly hairless. A Sphynx is covered in a fine down like the skin of a peach, warm and soft to the touch, with a body heat you feel at once. Big bat ears, a wrinkled face, and large lemon-shaped eyes give it a look that people either adore or find startling.

That bare skin needs care. Without a coat to absorb them, skin oils build up, so a Sphynx needs regular bathing and warm spots to curl into. It feels the cold and will burrow under blankets or against your neck.

The personality is the real reason for its rise. The Sphynx is an attention-seeking extrovert, energetic, clownish, and relentlessly affectionate, the cat most likely to greet your guests and supervise your every move. It is often called the most dog-like cat of all.

A Sphynx is high-maintenance in surprising ways. With no coat to absorb them, skin oils build up and leave a waxy film, so most need a wipe-down or a bath every week or two, along with regular ear and nail cleaning. They burn energy fast and feel the cold, so they seek out sweaters, sunbeams, and laps.

In temperament it is pure extrovert, demanding, comic, and devoted, the cat most likely to wake you for attention and least happy left alone. The breed can carry the heart condition HCM and a skin and gum disorder, so good breeders screen, and the cat needs warmth, calories, and company to thrive.
rc: The famous hairless cat, a fixture of CFA's top fifteen
f: Origin Of The Name
Named for its resemblance to the bald, ancient look of Egyptian sphinx statues, though the breed is modern and Canadian.
A Natural Mutation
The breed grew from a single hairless kitten born in Toronto in 1966, bred carefully for health.
Good To Know
It needs warmth, regular bathing to manage skin oils, and lots of company. It is not hypoallergenic, since it still produces the usual cat allergen.
Coat & Color
Effectively bald, with a soft peach-fuzz down and visible skin in many colors and patterns, often wrinkled around the face.
By the Numbers
Among the most recognizable cats in the world and a steady presence near the top of CFA registrations.
Living With One
Bathe regularly, keep it warm, and never leave it lonely. The Sphynx is needy, playful, and endlessly involved in your day.
Health Notes
Can carry the heart condition HCM. Wipe the skin to manage oils, clean the ears often, and choose screened breeders.
d: The Sphynx is not hairless. It wears a fine down, as soft as a peach.
The breed began with one hairless kitten born in Toronto in 1966.
The name nods to Egyptian statues, but the Sphynx is a modern Canadian cat.
Warm skin, a knitted blanket, and no plans. The Sphynx knows where the heat is.
A cold window is for looking. A warm bed is for living. Choose wisely.
Ask who greeted the guests and supervised the unpacking. The Sphynx did.
An elder Sphynx in a nest of wool. Still the warmest thing in the house.
lw: Snow outside, wool all around, and one cream cat settled at last.

The Sphynx has followed you from room to room all week and kept every lap warm. Now it sits on the quilt by the window, eyes half closed, a small heater with ears. Tomorrow it will want company again.

p: The teddy bear in a tweed coat. Britain's sturdy, dignified original.
s: The British Shorthair is the founding cat of Britain, descended from the working cats the Romans are said to have carried to the island to guard their grain. For centuries it was simply the British street and farm cat, before fanciers turned it into the plush, round-faced breed seen today.

It is built like a brick. A broad round head, full cheeks, big copper eyes, and a stocky cobby body sit under a dense, crisp coat that stands away from the skin. The blue-grey version, the British Blue, is so iconic that many people think it is the only color.

The temperament is famously easygoing. British Shorthairs are calm, dignified, and a little reserved, affectionate without being clingy. They will keep you company from across the room rather than demanding a lap, and they tolerate being left alone better than most.

Their plush looks have made them cultural icons. The breed is often named as the inspiration for the Cheshire Cat and for Puss in Boots. Easy to live with and slow to anger, the British Shorthair is one of the most popular cats in Britain and a steady climber in America.

The British Shorthair is one of the easiest cats to live with. It is calm, undemanding, and content to keep you company from its own chosen spot, tolerating time alone better than most and rarely making a fuss. It is not a natural lap cat and often prefers to sit beside you rather than on you.

Two things need watching. The dense coat sheds and wants regular brushing, more in spring, and the breed loves its food and gains weight easily, so portions matter. Like many breeds it can carry the heart condition HCM, and the kidney condition PKD appears in some lines, so good breeders test.
rc: Britain's plush original, a steady top-ten cat (CFA)
f: Origin Of The Name
Simply the shorthaired cat of Britain, the island's native working cat refined into a breed.
A Working Past
Descended from the rodent-catching cats of farms and streets, said to trace back to cats brought by the Romans.
Good To Know
Independent and undemanding, it likes company without needing a lap. The dense coat needs regular brushing, and the breed can run heavy, so watch the diet.
Coat & Color
A short, dense, crisp coat in many colors, with the blue-grey British Blue the signature look.
By the Numbers
Often cited as the model for the Cheshire Cat and Puss in Boots, and one of the most popular breeds in the United Kingdom.
Living With One
Brush the dense coat regularly and watch the waistline. Independent and tidy, it suits owners who want an easygoing companion.
Health Notes

p: America's working cat made good. A hardy, easygoing all-rounder.
s: The American Shorthair earned its place the hard way. Its ancestors came over on ships with the first European settlers, brought along to protect food stores from rats and mice. For generations they were simply the sturdy working cats of farms, barns, and homes across the country.

Fanciers eventually recognized that this hardy native cat deserved a standard of its own, and developed it into a breed while keeping its rugged good health. The result is a solid, muscular, medium-to-large cat with a broad face and a dense coat, the classic silver tabby being the best known.

The temperament is the breed's calling card. American Shorthairs are easygoing, adaptable, and friendly, equally happy to play or to settle in beside you. They get along with children, dogs, and other cats, and they tolerate change with unusual grace.

They are also famously healthy and long-lived, a legacy of generations of natural selection as working cats. CFA recognized the breed in 1906, originally as the Domestic Shorthair, and it remains one of America's favorite cats.

The American Shorthair earns its keep as the low-maintenance family cat. It is adaptable and undemanding, equally at home with children, dogs, and quiet retirees, and it takes the comings and goings of a busy household in stride. A weekly brush is about all the coat asks.

Its working-cat heritage shows in robust health and a long life, often into the high teens. The main risks are a tendency to put on weight without enough play and, as in many breeds, a chance of the heart condition HCM, so measured meals, active games, and regular checkups keep it thriving.
rc: America's hardy native, a top-ten cat (CFA)
f: Origin Of The Name
The shorthaired working cat of America, formalized from the country's everyday house and barn cats.
A Working Past
Descended from cats carried on ships to control rodents, prized for centuries for hardiness rather than looks.
Good To Know
Adaptable and tolerant, it suits families, other pets, and busy homes. Easy to groom and generally robust, though it can gain weight if overfed.
Coat & Color
A short, thick, hard coat in many colors and patterns, with the silver classic tabby the signature look.
By the Numbers
Recognized by CFA in 1906, originally as the Domestic Shorthair. Known for long life and sturdy health.
Living With One
Easy on every front. Brush weekly, keep it playing, and it fits almost any home and any age of owner.
Health Notes
Hardy and long-lived, but prone to weight gain and, in some lines, the heart condition HCM, so manage diet and screen where possible.
